claims.text: Residual Mg supersaturation is present in the as-cast, non-equilibrium alloy.
Residual Mg supersaturation promotes formation of metastable Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
The metastable Mg-rich phases later decompose into more stable intermetallic compounds.
Decomposition of the metastable phases produces refined microstructural features.
The phase evolution changes the development and chemistry of the surface oxide or passivation layer.
A protective Mg-enriched oxide scale enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The evolved multiphase microstructure creates galvanic micro-couples that exacerbate localized corrosion.
The initial as-cast MgAlCuZnGd-type alloy contains a mixture of solid solution and early-stage metastable intermetallic phases.
Annealing drives metastable Mg-rich intermetallics toward stable phases.
The transformation changes grain-boundary chemistry and phase distribution.
During heat treatment, excess Mg segregates and forms stable intermetallic compounds.
The altered microstructure promotes formation of a more coherent Mg-enriched oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation.
Compositional heterogeneity causes galvanic interactions during aqueous corrosion.
Interfaces between electrochemically dissimilar phases can act as anodic corrosion sites.
Relative to the as-cast material, the heat-treated alloy will form a thicker, more adherent, and more protective oxidation scale.
Relative to the as-cast material, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit increased localized corrosion.
The initial mixed-phase microstructure is generated by rapid solidification and inherent Mg supersaturation.
The proposed mechanism applies below a density of 6 g/cm3 when sufficient Mg is present to form metastable phases and non-equilibrium phases persist initially.
